result:
The night sky has always been humanity's oldest library. Long before we invented writing, we invented stories to explain the lights overhead: hunters, gods, animals frozen in eternal chase. Those stories were wrong in the details, of course, but they were right in the impulse. We looked up and refused to accept that the lights were merely lights.

Today the stories have better instruments. We know the nearest star is four years away at the speed of light, that the Milky Way is a barred spiral containing hundreds of billions of suns, that most of those suns probably host planets, and that a non-trivial fraction of those planets sit in the temperate zone where liquid water can persist. We know the universe is 13.8 billion years old and still expanding, that space itself is stretching, that the farthest galaxies we see are receding faster than light because the space between us and them is growing. We know that most of the matter in the cosmos does not interact with light at all.

None of this knowledge has diminished the wonder. If anything it has sharpened it. The same sky that once inspired myths now inspires equations, and the equations keep revealing stranger myths: black holes that warp time, quantum fields that fluctuate into particles, a possible multiverse in which every possible history plays out. The universe is not only larger than we imagined; it is stranger than we can currently imagine.

That strangeness is a gift. It means there will always be more to learn, more to see, more to become. Curiosity is not a luxury; it is the oldest survival strategy we have, now applied to questions that no longer threaten our immediate existence but still define what kind of species we choose to be. We can stay on one small rock and argue about the same old things, or we can keep looking up.

I choose the latter. The lights are still there. They are still waiting. And we are still the only known creatures who bother to ask what they mean.
